    Diagnostics

    Every finding the tool reports carries an identifier. It is NGA and four digits, and it never changes meaning. This chapter lists all of them.

    Read it when the tool said something you want to look up. Do not read it in order.

    How to read a finding

    error[NGA5205]: `level.map` is loaded from storage, and cannot live where the
                stream reads through, at $4000
 --> main.ngp:12:3

    The identifier comes first. The message follows, with the names of the program written into it. The location points at the line that caused the finding, and a finding about the whole program has no location.

    The number says which part of the tool raised it, so the number alone says where to look. The tables below are grouped that way.

    A number is never reused. A diagnostic that is retired takes its number with it.

    Severity

    An error stops the build at the next gate. A warning does not stop anything. A note never stands alone and always explains the finding above it.

    The severity in the tables is the default. A Project changes it in its diagnostics block, and the command line changes it with --deny, --allow and --off. The command line wins.

    What the message shows here

    The tables show the message as the tool holds it, with named arguments in braces. A real finding has values there instead. So `{section}` is pinned at {address:hex} is printed as `hud` is pinned at $2000.

    Below the tables, every finding has an entry: when the tool raises it, and what to do about it. Most entries show a small program that raises it, with what the tool printed for it. An example that shows no Project file is built with one that names its Modules and nothing else. An identifier in the tables links to its entry.

    Index

    The identifiers by the part of the tool that raises them.

    NGA7265 error {name} is a reserved Region, which C does not reach
    NGA7267 note {name} is defined here
    NGA7268 error {name} takes or returns u8[N], bytes that a call from C does not hand over
    NGA7269 error {name} is defined in C, and extern declares only what the assembler exports
    NGA7270 error {name} is declared extern, and nothing the assembler exports is named so
    NGA7271 error {name} is declared extern already, and a name is declared once in the program
    NGA7272 error {name} is declared extern, and {what}
    NGA7273 error {name} {what}
    NGA7274 error {name} reads past what the assembler wrote as data: {reason}
    NGA7275 error {path}, at offset {offset}, splits an item the assembler wrote
    NGA7276 error {what} holds {value}, which is no {type}
    NGA7277 error {name} {what}
    NGA7278 error {name} is no character set, and a literal's prefix names one
    NGA7279 error {name} is {what}, and {form} takes {takes}
    NGA7280 error {name} is in family {family}, whose member is known at run time alone: call it in a with({family}, i) block
    NGA7281 error {name} is in pane {pane} of window {window}, which this block shows in another state: the call's .with would leave that pane shown, not the block's
    NGA7282 error window {window} is shown by the block this one stands in, and a window shows one state at a time
    NGA7283 error {keyword} leaves the with block, which would leave the window as the block shows it
    NGA7284 error the address of {name}, in what this block shows, is kept only in a local of the block or handed to a call in it: here it {escapes}
    NGA7286 error the index of with({name}, i) is {what}, and X takes a u8 or a constant
    NGA7287 error [[{attribute}]] takes {takes}
    NGA7288 error {name} is [[in]] a pane and [[under]] one, and code under a pane is in none
    NGA7289 error this block shows another state of window {window} from code in pane {pane}, which cannot switch its own window: write [[with(...), trampoline]], and pay a Proc in fixed and a jsr
    NGA7290 error trampoline on a block that needs none: {where}, and the block is a macro under .with
    NGA7291 error this block shows {pane}, and the code is in {pane} already
    NGA7292 error {name} is in pane {pane} of window {window}, and this code is in pane {own} of it, which cannot switch its own window: call it in a [[with({pane}), trampoline]] block or an [[under({own})]] function
    NGA7293 error {name} runs under pane {pane}, called from code in the pane, from another function under it, or in a block that shows it, and this is none
    NGA7294 error a transition enters a phase and never comes back, so it stands on a bare return in a void function, and {what}
    NGA7295 error {name} is a slot, and its binding is its type's: a function binds a vector and a T* const a pointer, and {what}
    NGA7296 error {name} fills slot {slot}, whose cell holds an address the program reads as {wanted}, and {what}
    NGA7297 error {name} is no {type}: {what}
    NGA7298 error {name} is taken as {type} here and as {other} elsewhere, and a function reads its arguments from one place
    NGA7299 error {name} names a function type, which is a type only as a pointer: {name}*
    NGA7300 error this call is of the function type its caller is a member of, which would write the temporaries the caller reads; a member dispatches through another type, or through a name
    NGA7301 error {name} is written auto and given {what}, which takes its type from where it is used and so has none to give
    NGA7302 error {name} is written inline and cannot be wrapped into its caller: it {what}
    NGA7303 error inline is written on {what}, which has no body to wrap into a caller
    NGA7304 error {name} is assigned by {operator} where it is used as a value, and reached again in the same expression, which is an order the subset does not fix
    NGA7305 error {name} is a pointer, which (zp),y reads through, so it lies in the zero page whatever is asked
    NGA7306 error {name} lies in stripes, whose place its layout settles, so [[placement]] is a second answer
    NGA7307 warning {name} is {class} already, so this says nothing
    NGA7308 error {name} is read here before anything writes it, and a static local holds what was there; give it a value where it is declared
    NGA7309 error {name} is a name in a Namespace, and C defines none there; :: reads what the assembler exports
    NGA7310 error a plain assignment is a statement and not a value: write two assignments; a compound one, such as +=, is a value
    NGA7311 error {name} is const and given constants, so it is read-only data, which lies off the zero page whatever is asked
    NGA7312 warning {name} is const and given a constant, so it takes no byte, and [[placement]] has nothing to place

    Every diagnostic

    One entry per identifier, in the order of their numbers.

    NGA0001

    error · unexpected character {character}

    Outside strings and comments, an .asm Module or a Project file holds ASCII letters, digits and the punctuation of the language. Any other character there raises this, such as a backslash or a non-ASCII letter. Typographic quotes pasted from a word processor are a common case.

    .section
title   .byte “HELLO”
.ends

    error[NGA0001]: unexpected character `“`
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 | title   .byte “HELLO”
  |               ^

error[NGA0001]: unexpected character `”`
 --> main.asm:2:23
  |
2 | title   .byte “HELLO”
  |                     ^

    Type the ASCII character that was meant, here ".

    NGA0002

    error · unterminated string literal

    A string literal is still open where the file ends: the last line lacks its closing ", and no line ending follows it. The same mistake on any other line is NGA0003. Close the string.

    NGA0003

    error · string literal is not closed before the end of the line

    A string literal ends on the line it starts on, and this one reaches the end of its line without a closing ". There is no line continuation. Everything after the opening quote belongs to the string, a ; comment included.

    .section
title   .byte "PRESS START
.ends

    error[NGA0003]: string literal is not closed before the end of the line
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 | title   .byte "PRESS START
  |               ^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Close the string. A longer text is several strings, on one .byte line or on several.

    NGA0004

    error · unterminated character literal

    A character literal opens with ' and is not closed before the end of its line. An apostrophe inside one is written \'.

    .proc entry
        lda #'A
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0004]: unterminated character literal
 --> main.asm:2:14
  |
2 |         lda #'A
  |              ^^

    Close it: 'A'.

    NGA0005

    error · character literal is empty

    A character literal stands for the value of one character, and '' holds none. For a space write ' ', and for the zero byte '\0' or 0. An apostrophe is '\'': ''' reads as an empty literal followed by an open one.

    .section
blank   .byte ''
.ends

    error[NGA0005]: character literal is empty
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 | blank   .byte ''
  |               ^^

    NGA0006

    error · character literal holds more than one character

    A character literal is the value of one character. An escape such as '\n' counts as one. For several bytes, write a string: .byte "AB".

    .section
keys    .byte 'AB'
.ends

    error[NGA0006]: character literal holds more than one character
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 | keys    .byte 'AB'
  |               ^^^^

    NGA0007

    error · unknown escape sequence \{escape}

    A backslash in a string or a character literal starts an escape. The escapes are \\, \", \', \n, \t and \0. There is no \xNN and no \r.

    .section
prompt  .byte "READY\x9B"
.ends

    error[NGA0007]: unknown escape sequence `\x`
 --> main.asm:2:21
  |
2 | prompt  .byte "READY\x9B"
  |                     ^^

    A byte no escape spells goes beside the string in the data directive: .byte "READY", $9B.

    NGA0009

    error · invalid UTF-8 encoding

    Raised inside a comment, a string or a character literal whose bytes are not UTF-8. Outside them, such a byte is NGA0001. A comment or a literal reports it once. The usual cause is a file saved in a legacy code page with accented letters in its comments. Save the file as UTF-8.

    NGA0010

    error · {prefix} is not followed by any digits

    $ begins a hexadecimal number and % a binary one, and here no digit follows. The language has no remainder operator, so % written as one raises this.

    COUNT = 20

.proc entry
        lda #COUNT % 8
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0010]: `%` is not followed by any digits
 --> main.asm:4:20
  |
4 |         lda #COUNT % 8
  |                    ^

    For a power of two, COUNT & 7 is the remainder of division by 8.

    NGA0011

    error · {character} is not valid in a {base} literal

    A number has one base: decimal with no prefix, hexadecimal after $, binary after %. Raised for a digit the base does not have, such as 2 after %, and for a letter that touches a number, which is read as one of its digits. 0FFh, the notation of other assemblers, is read as a decimal number, and F is not a decimal digit.

    .proc entry
        lda #0FFh
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0011]: `F` is not valid in a decimal literal
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 |         lda #0FFh
  |               ^

    Write $FF. A number reports this once, however many of its digits are wrong.

    NGA0012

    error · _ in a numeric literal must stand between digits

    A _ groups the digits of a number, as in %1010_0101 or 65_536. It needs a digit on each side: it cannot follow the prefix, end the number, or stand next to another _.

    .section
mask    .byte %_1010_0101
.ends

    error[NGA0012]: `_` in a numeric literal must stand between digits
 --> main.asm:2:16
  |
2 | mask    .byte %_1010_0101
  |                ^

    A number reports this once, however many separators are misplaced in it.

    NGA0013

    error · hexadecimal literals are written $1F, not 0x1F

    Hexadecimal is written with $. 0x is C's notation, and neither an .asm Module nor a Project file takes it. A .ngc Module does.

    .proc entry
        lda #0x1F
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0013]: hexadecimal literals are written `$1F`, not `0x1F`
 --> main.asm:2:14
  |
2 |         lda #0x1F
  |              ^^^^

    NGA0014

    error · numeric local labels do not exist; use @, @+, @-, or a name

    A local label is named, @loop, or anonymous, @. A digit after @, @+ or @- is refused: @1 is not a name, and @-2 does not count two labels back.

    .proc entry
        ldx #8
@1      dex
        bne @1
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0014]: numeric local labels do not exist; use `@`, `@+`, `@-`, or a name
 --> main.asm:3:1
  |
3 | @1      dex
  | ^^

error[NGA0014]: numeric local labels do not exist; use `@`, `@+`, `@-`, or a name
 --> main.asm:4:13
  |
4 |         bne @1
  |             ^^

    Name the label, or write @ and reach the nearest one with @- or @+. See Local labels.

    NGA0015

    error · control character {code:hex} in source

    A control character, a byte below $20 or the byte $7F, stands outside a string, a character literal and a comment. Tab, line feed and carriage return are allowed. The usual cause is a form feed or another byte left by an editor or a file conversion. Delete it; the location shows where. The line quoted under the message shows the byte as its symbol from Unicode's Control Pictures, ␀ for a NUL and ␌ for a form feed.

    NGA0016

    error · this number is too large to be represented

    The tool computes with signed 64-bit integers, so the largest literal is $7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF.

    .section
big     .word $1_0000_0000_0000_0000
.ends

    error[NGA0016]: this number is too large to be represented
 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 | big     .word $1_0000_0000_0000_0000
  |               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    A value that is representable but does not fit the byte or word it is written to is NGA6101.

    NGA0017

    error · a leading zero does not make {literal} octal; write it in decimal, $ or %

    A decimal literal of more than one digit starts with 0. C reads such a literal as octal, so 017 is 15 there and 17 to anyone who never learned C. The tool takes neither reading. 0 alone is zero, and a 0 after $ or % is an ordinary digit.

    .proc entry
        ldx #017
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0017]: a leading zero does not make `017` octal; write it in decimal, `$` or `%`
 --> main.asm:2:14
  |
2 |         ldx #017
  |              ^^^

    Drop the zero, ldx #17, or write the value in hexadecimal or binary, ldx #$0F. The same rule in a .ngc Module is NGA7006.

    NGA0100

    error · expected an expression

    The grammar needs a value here and finds none. Typical causes are an operand left out, as in lda #, a comma at the end of a list of data, and * written for the current address, which the language does not have. Put a Label where an address is wanted.

    .section
table   .byte 1, 2, 3,
.ends

    error[NGA0100]: expected an expression
 --> main.asm:2:23
  |
2 | table   .byte 1, 2, 3,
  |                       ^

    NGA0101

    error · expected ) to close this parenthesis

    A ( in an expression or an operand has no ) before the end of the line. The location is the ( left open.

    WIDTH = 40

.proc entry
        lda #(WIDTH * 2
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0101]: expected `)` to close this parenthesis
 --> main.asm:4:14
  |
4 |         lda #(WIDTH * 2
  |              ^

    NGA0102

    error · << is a shift; the low byte of an operand is <

    < in front of an operand takes its low byte, and > its high byte. << is the left shift and needs a value on each side. Written in front of an operand it is read as <, so nothing else is reported.

    .proc entry
        lda #<<screen
        rts
.endp

.section
screen  .res 40
.ends

    error[NGA0102]: `<<` is a shift; the low byte of an operand is `<`
 --> main.asm:2:14
  |
2 |         lda #<<screen
  |              ^^

    Remove one <.

    NGA0103

    error · {outer} and {inner} need parentheses to say which one binds first

    Two pairs of operators are refused without parentheses: a shift with + or -, and &, | or ^ with a comparison. C gives both an order that is often not the one meant: it reads a & $FF == 0 as a & ($FF == 0). The tool names the two operators and does not choose.

    ROWS = 24

.proc entry
        lda #ROWS + 1 << 2
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0103]: `<<` and `+` need parentheses to say which one binds first
 --> main.asm:4:14
  |
4 |         lda #ROWS + 1 << 2
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Add the parentheses for the reading you mean, (ROWS + 1) << 2 or ROWS + (1 << 2). See Precedence.

    NGA0104

    error · this expression nests more than {limit} deep

    An expression nests at most 64 operators deep, and at most 64 parentheses deep, the two counted apart. A chain such as 1+1+1 counts each operator, so a long sum written term by term reaches the limit. Split it into Constants that each hold a part: the limit applies to each expression on its own.

    NGA0110

    error · {token} cannot begin a statement

    A statement begins with a mnemonic, a macro's name or a directive. At column one a line may also begin with a Label or a Constant. Raised for a line that begins with anything else. Two common cases come from other assemblers: *= $2000 to set the address, and a comment written with //.

    *= $2000

.proc entry
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0110]: `*` cannot begin a statement
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | *= $2000
  | ^

    A comment starts with ;. A Section says where it goes with an attribute, .section absolute at $2000, or names no address and the solver picks one. See Placement.

    NGA0111

    error · unexpected {token} after the end of the statement

    A statement ends where its grammar is complete, and the rest of its line is empty or a ; comment. Raised for whatever follows: most often a comma missing between two values, or a second statement on the same line, as in lda #1 : sta $80. A line holds one statement. Not raised for a token the lexer refused, such as % 8, which has a finding of its own.

    .section
table   .byte 1, 2 3
.ends

    error[NGA0111]: unexpected `3` after the end of the statement
 --> main.asm:2:20
  |
2 | table   .byte 1, 2 3
  |                    ^

    NGA0112

    error · {name} at column one defines a label; indent it to write an instruction

    A name at column one is a Label, and what follows it on the line must be a statement. Raised where it cannot be one. Usually an instruction with an operand has lost its indentation: lda #0 at column one is a Label lda followed by #0, and also gets NGA0113. A Label written with a colon, as other assemblers write one, is NGA0199 instead.

    .proc entry
lda #0
        sta $D01A
        rts
.endp

    warning[NGA0113]: `lda` at column one defines a label named like an instruction
 --> main.asm:2:1
  |
2 | lda #0
  | ^^^

error[NGA0112]: `lda` at column one defines a label; indent it to write an instruction
 --> main.asm:2:1
  |
2 | lda #0
  | ^^^

    Indent the instruction.

    NGA0113

    warning · {name} at column one defines a label named like an instruction

    A label in column one that is spelled like an instruction is almost always an instruction that lost its indentation. The tool cannot tell the two apart, because a label is marked by position and nothing else.

    .proc entry
        lda #0
        sta $0600
rts
.endp

    warning[NGA4612]: control runs off the end of `entry` into whatever is placed after it: end it with a jump or a return, or chain a proc to it with `then`
 --> main.asm:3:9
  |
3 |         sta $0600
  |         ^^^^^^^^^

warning[NGA0113]: `rts` at column one defines a label named like an instruction
 --> main.asm:4:1
  |
4 | rts
  | ^^^

    Here the rts became a label, and the Proc now runs off its end. Indent the line. Where a label is meant to be named like this, turn the warning off on the line below with .off NGA0113. A Proc's name is not such a label: .proc inc names it after a directive, which no lost indent writes, so it draws nothing, and a C function called inc is written that way.

    NGA0114

    error · a direction marks a reference, not a definition

    @- and @+ belong to a reference, where they choose the nearest definition before or after it. A definition is @name or @ alone.

    .proc entry
        ldx #8
@-loop  dex
        bne @-loop
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0114]: a direction marks a reference, not a definition
 --> main.asm:3:1
  |
3 | @-loop  dex
  | ^^^^^^

error[NGA2210]: no definition of `@loop` matches this reference
 --> main.asm:4:13
  |
4 |         bne @-loop
  |             ^^^^^^

    Write the definition without the sign. Since this one is refused, the reference below it finds no @loop, which is NGA2210.

    NGA0115

    error · a local label has no scope outside a .proc

    A local label, @name or @, takes its scope from the .proc or the macro body it stands in. In a .section or at the top level of a Module there is none, and the definition and every reference are refused.

    .section
clear   ldx #0
@loop   sta $0600,x
        inx
        bne @loop
        rts
.ends

    error[NGA0115]: a local label has no scope outside a `.proc`
 --> main.asm:3:1
  |
3 | @loop   sta $0600,x
  | ^^^^^

error[NGA0115]: a local label has no scope outside a `.proc`
 --> main.asm:5:13
  |
5 |         bne @loop
  |             ^^^^^

    Write the code as a .proc, or give the label a plain name. See Local labels.

    NGA0116

    error · .declare says what a byte of a proc is, and this stands outside one

    .declare makes a Temporary of a Proc an argument or the result. It stands inside the .proc, on the line above the .ztemp or .temp it names.

            .declare arg u8
value   .ztemp 1

.proc twice
        lda value
        asl
        sta value
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0116]: `.declare` says what a byte of a proc is, and this stands outside one
 --> main.asm:1:9
  |
1 |         .declare arg u8
  |         ^^^^^^^^

    Move both lines into the Proc. See .declare.

    NGA0117

    error · .declare says what the .ztemp or .temp below it is, and this is not one

    .declare applies to the next statement, which must be a .ztemp or a .temp. Only blank lines and comments may stand between. Raised where something else comes first, or nothing does.

    .proc twice
        .declare arg u8
        lda value
        asl
        sta value
        rts
value   .ztemp 1
.endp

    error[NGA0117]: `.declare` says what the `.ztemp` or `.temp` below it is, and this is not one
 --> main.asm:2:9
  |
2 |         .declare arg u8
  |         ^^^^^^^^

    Move the .declare to the line above its reservation. A .declare that keeps every byte in a register, as .declare arg a, takes no reservation and is not held to this.

    NGA0118

    error · .declare says arg or ret, found {token}

    The word after .declare is the role: arg for an argument, ret for the result. A type or a place may follow it, as in .declare arg u8.

    .proc twice
        .declare u8
value   .ztemp 1
        lda value
        asl
        sta value
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0118]: `.declare` says `arg` or `ret`, found `u8`
 --> main.asm:2:18
  |
2 |         .declare u8
  |                  ^^

    NGA0119

    error · {name} is not a type or a place; a declared byte is u8, i8, u16, i16, bool or u8[N], or a place is a letter a byte from the low one: a, x or y, and m for memory beside one of them

    After arg or ret comes a type, a place, or nothing. The count of u8[N] is a number written out, from 1 to 65535, and a Constant's name is refused there. A place is one or two letters, one per byte from the low one, and at least one of them names a register.

    LENGTH = 4

.proc clear
        .declare arg u8[LENGTH]
buffer  .ztemp LENGTH
        lda #0
        sta buffer
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0119]: `u8[LENGTH]` is not a type or a place; a declared byte is `u8`, `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `bool` or `u8[N]`, or a place is a letter a byte from the low one: `a`, `x` or `y`, and `m` for memory beside one of them
 --> main.asm:4:22
  |
4 |         .declare arg u8[LENGTH]
  |                      ^^

    Where the size is a Constant, write no type. The size of the reservation then gives it, so .declare arg over buffer .ztemp LENGTH is a u8[4].

    NGA0120

    error · unknown directive .{name}

    A directive is a . and one of the words listed in The assembler. The usual cause is a directive of another assembler. .org has no counterpart: a Section says where it goes with .section absolute at $2000, or the solver places it. .db and .dw are .byte and .word. A file that .include would read is a Module of its own, named in the Project's modules block, and a binary file is a binary( "file.bin" ) entry there.

    .org $2000

.proc entry
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA0120]: unknown directive `.org`
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .org $2000
  | ^^^^

    NGA0121

    error · .end does not say what it closes; write the block's own closer: .ends, .endp, .endm, .endif, .endmatch, .endns or .endch

    Each block has its own closer: .ends, .endp, .endm, .endif, .endns, .endch and .endmatch, and .end is none of them. The block stays open, so it is also reported as never closed.

    .proc entry
        rts
.end

    error[NGA0125]: this `.proc` is never closed
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .proc entry
  | ^^^^^

error[NGA0121]: `.end` does not say what it closes; write the block's own closer: `.ends`, `.endp`, `.endm`, `.endif`, `.endmatch`, `.endns` or `.endch`
 --> main.asm:3:1
  |
3 | .end
  | ^^^^

    Where .end marks the end of the source, as in other assemblers, delete it: a Module ends where its file does. See Abbreviations.

    NGA0122

    error · expected a name after {after}

    The grammar needs a name here and finds something else, or the end of the line. Raised after a directive that declares or names something, such as .proc, .macro, .namespace, .slot or .transition; after then at .endp; after in, under or as among a Section's attributes; and after a . with no word behind it. A number or a string is not a name.

    .proc entry
        rts
.endp then

    error[NGA0122]: expected a name after `then`
 --> main.asm:3:7
  |
3 | .endp then
  |       ^^^^

    NGA0123

    error · {name} is not a section attribute

    A Section's attributes are a placement, root, in NAME, temporary, readonly and foreign, and a .proc adds under NAME and as NAME. at, align and within are not attributes. They complete a placement, so they stand right after zeropage or absolute, with no comma.

    .section at $2000
table   .byte 1, 2, 3
.ends

    error[NGA0123]: `at` is not a section attribute
 --> main.asm:1:10
  |
1 | .section at $2000
  |          ^^

    Write .section absolute at $2000. The word is dropped together with what follows it up to the next comma, here $2000, and the Section opens with the attributes that are left. What it holds and its .ends are read as usual. See Placement.

    NGA0124

    error · this .section is never closed

    A .section closes with .ends before the end of the file, and one opened inside a .proc closes before its .endp. The finding stands at the .section left open.

    .proc entry
        inc counter
        rts
.section
counter .byte 0
.endp

    error[NGA0124]: this `.section` is never closed
 --> main.asm:4:1
  |
4 | .section
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Add the .ends.

    NGA0125

    error · this .proc is never closed

    A .proc closes with .endp before the end of the file. The finding stands at the .proc left open. A .endp inside an .if branch is refused, NGA0169, and leaves the Proc open.

    .proc entry
        rts

Residency is per Module, so this is raised where the follower's Module is present in a Phase and the code's Module is not: here a resident dispatcher and a routine of game. Reported once per taking and follower, for the first such Phase.

    main.ngp

    modules { "main.asm" "game.asm" }

resident { main }

phase game { needs game  then over  entry gameStart }
phase over { entry gameOver }
entry game

    main.asm

    .export dispatch, ptr

.section zeropage
ptr     .res 2
.ends

.proc dispatch
        jmp (ptr)
.endp

.proc gameOver
@stop   jmp @stop
.endp

    game.asm

    .proc gameStart
        lda handler
        sta ptr
        lda handler + 1
        sta ptr + 1
        jsr dispatch
        .transition over
        .own dispatch
handler .word step
.endp

.proc step
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA4611]: `step` is handed to `dispatch`, which is present in phase `over` where `step` is not: a jump from there would land in nothing
 --> game.asm:9:9
  |
9 | handler .word step
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^

    Hand the address to a follower in the code's own Module, which is present exactly where the code is, or make the code's Module present wherever the follower is. Under a bare .own the follower is the Section that takes the address, and the same mistake is NGA2414.

    NGA4612

    warning · control runs off the end of {section} into whatever is placed after it: end it with a jump or a return, or chain a proc to it with then

    Sections are placed independently, so control that runs past the last statement of one goes into whatever the solver put after it. Raised at the statement some run leaves from: an instruction that goes on, a call of a routine that may return, a branch to the end of the Section, or code that runs into data.

    .proc entry
        jsr init
.endp

.proc init
        rts
.endp

    warning[NGA4612]: control runs off the end of `entry` into whatever is placed after it: end it with a jump or a return, or chain a proc to it with `then`
 --> main.asm:2:9
  |
2 |         jsr init
  |         ^^^^^^^^

    A brk ends a Section as a return or a jump does. To fall into the next Proc on purpose, chain it with .endp then NAME, which the solver places right after. Where a branch at the end is always taken, .off NGA4612 on it says so.

    NGA4613

    error · phase {phase} is final, and {entry}, where it is entered, may return: nothing is kept there for a return to land on

    A final Phase is one the program never leaves. The tool keeps out of it the code that runs only when the program ends or returns. A return from the Phase's entry would land in that code, which is not there.

    main.ngp

    modules { "main.asm" }

phase game { needs main  final }
entry game

    main.asm

    CONSOL = $D01F

.proc entry
@frame  lda CONSOL
        cmp #6
        bne @frame
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA4613]: phase `game` is final, and `entry`, where it is entered, may return: nothing is kept there for a return to land on
 --> main.ngp:3:26
  |
3 | phase game { needs main  final }
  |                          ^^^^^

    End every path of the entry in a loop that does not return, or drop final.

    NGA4614

    error · {name} is no holder: a target declares the hardware that holds a section with holder

    .root and .release name a Holder: hardware that holds one Section at a time, which the Target declares with holder. atari/800xl.ngp and atari/130xe.ngp declare nine, from dlist to dosini. The stand-in Target declares none.

    .proc entry
        .root dlist
        lda #<list
        rts
.endp

.section
list    .byte $70
.ends

 --> main.asm:2:15
  |
2 |         .root dlist
  |               ^^^^^

    Include the variant of the machine, or declare the Holder in a target block of the Project, target { holder dlist }. See Roots.

    NGA5102

    error · {mnemonic} has no {mode} form

    The processor has no instruction for this mnemonic and this operand. Either the form does not exist at all, as sta #1, or it exists for one PlacementClass only: stx takes ,y and sty takes ,x only with a zero-page operand. The message names the form that is missing: absolute,y where only the zero-page form exists, as here, and direct,y where neither width has one.

    .section
buffer  .res 16
.ends

.proc entry
        ldy #0
        stx buffer,y
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA5102]: `stx` has no absolute,y form
 --> main.asm:7:9
  |
7 |         stx buffer,y
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^

    buffer is absolute. Put it in a .section zeropage, or go through A with txa and sta buffer,y.

    NGA5103

    error · the placement class of this operand cannot be determined, so its width cannot be either

    An operand without # that is an Integer has no PlacementClass, so its value decides whether the instruction is zero page or absolute. That value has to be a declared value, known before any Section has an address. tableEnd - table is an Integer with Labels at its leaves, and has a value only after Size.

    .section
table   .byte 1, 2, 3
tableEnd
.ends

.proc entry
        ldx #0
@loop   lda table,x
        inx
        cpx tableEnd - table
        bne @loop
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA5103]: the placement class of this operand cannot be determined, so its width cannot be either
  --> main.asm:10:13
   |
10 |         cpx tableEnd - table
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Here the # is missing: cpx #tableEnd - table compares with the count. Where an address is meant, write an Address, such as a Label plus an offset, which takes its Section's PlacementClass.

    NGA5104

    error · this size depends on itself

    The count of a .res may be written in terms of other sizes, such as work.runtimeSectionSize or the distance between two Labels. Raised where following those sizes leads back to the reservation itself.

    .section
buffer  .res buffer.runtimeSectionSize
.ends

    error[NGA5104]: this size depends on itself
 --> main.asm:2:9
  |
2 | buffer  .res buffer.runtimeSectionSize
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    A cycle through several Sections is reported once, at one of its reservations. Break it by writing one of the sizes as a Constant.

    NGA5105

    error · a reservation of {size:n} bytes is not a reservation

    .res takes a count from 0 to 65,536. A negative count usually comes from a subtraction of two Constants in the wrong order, or after one of them changed.

    ROWS = 24
VISIBLE = 25

.section
spare   .res ROWS - VISIBLE
.ends

    error[NGA5105]: a reservation of -1 bytes is not a reservation
 --> main.asm:5:9
  |
5 | spare   .res ROWS - VISIBLE
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    A Section that stands in a unit set declaring linear may reserve up to the size of the set's Banks end to end, which can exceed 64 KB.

    NGA5106

    error · {value:hex} is not an address

    An Integer operand without # is an address given by its value, so the value must lie between $0000 and $FFFF. It is usually a Constant with an offset added past the end of memory, or subtracted below zero.

    SCREEN = $F000

.proc entry
        lda SCREEN + $1000
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA5106]: $010000 is not an address
 --> main.asm:4:13
  |
4 |         lda SCREEN + $1000
  |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Check the Constant and the arithmetic on it.

    NGA5107

    error · {mnemonic} is a {needs} instruction, and this target is a {cpu}

    The Target says which processor the program is for, and a Target that names none is a 6502. The 65SC02's additions, such as stz, bra, phx and the (zp) modes, are refused on a 6502. So is an opcode of the 65SC02 that an .alt names.

    .section
counter .res 1
.ends

.proc entry
        stz counter
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA5107]: `stz` is a `65sc02` instruction, and this target is a `6502`
 --> main.asm:6:9
  |
6 |         stz counter
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^

    Where the machine has a 65SC02, write cpu "65sc02" in its target block; see the Project file. Otherwise write the 6502 form, here lda #0 and sta counter. See Instructions.

    NGA5201

    error · {section} overlaps {other} at {address:hex}

    Two pinned Sections claim the same bytes in a Phase both are present in. A pin is never moved, so the tool has no way to resolve it. The message names the Section reported and the pinned one it lands on.

    .section absolute at $3000
screen  .res 960
.ends

.section absolute at $3300
font    .res 1024
.ends

    error[NGA5201]: `font` overlaps `screen` at $3300
 --> main.asm:5:1
  |
5 | .section absolute at $3300
  | ^^^^^^^^

    screen reaches $33BF. Move one of the pins, or drop one and let the solver place that Section. Sections that are never in memory at the same time, such as reservations in Modules no Phase needs together, may be pinned at the same address.

    NGA5202

    error · there is no room for {section}, which needs {size:n} bytes

    Raised in two cases. A pinned Section runs past $FFFF. Or a Section that is not pinned is larger than every range of free memory it could start in, once its in, align and within are counted.

    .section
buffer  .res 40000
.ends

    error[NGA5202]: there is no room for `buffer`, which needs 40,000 bytes
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section
  | ^^^^^^^^

error[NGA5206]: no layout satisfies every constraint at once

error[NGA5631]: phase `(implicit)` does not fit in view `fixed`: requires 40,000 bytes, 32,768 available
note: `buffer` accounts for 40,000 bytes
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section
  | ^^^^^^^^

    The findings after it say the same thing for the whole program: no layout exists (NGA5206), and the Phase needs more memory than it has (NGA5631). With no region declared, the stand-in Target has 32 KB, at $2000-$9FFF. Make the Section smaller or split it. A zero-page Section that does not fit is NGA5204 instead.

    NGA5203

    error · a pin is a declared address, and {text} is {what}

    A pin is a declared value from $0000 to $FFFF, so no Label and no size may appear in it: a pin is part of the layout, and a Label's address is what the layout decides. In a Section that stands in a unit set declaring linear, the pin is a linear address and may be larger.

    .section absolute at $10000
table   .byte 1
.ends

    error[NGA5203]: a pin is a declared address, and `$10000` is past $FFFF
 --> main.asm:1:22
  |
1 | .section absolute at $10000
  |                      ^^^^^^

    NGA5204

    error · {section} is zero page and does not fit below $100

    A zeropage Section lies wholly below $100. Raised for a pin that makes it run past $FF, and for a Section that is not pinned and is larger than every free range of zero page the Target has.

    .section zeropage at $F0
ptrs    .res 32
.ends

    error[NGA5204]: `ptrs` is zero page and does not fit below $100
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section zeropage at $F0
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Pin it lower, split it, or move what does not need zero-page addressing into an absolute Section. With no region declared, the stand-in Target has 16 bytes of zero page, $80-$8F.

    NGA5205

    error · {section} is loaded from storage, and cannot live where the stream reads through, at {address:hex}

    The Window the driver's stream reads through is where storage arrives. A Section that waits in storage cannot also live at the address it arrives through, because the arrival would overwrite it while it is being read.

    main.ngp

    include "atari/130xe.ngp"
include "atari/extension.ngp"

modules { "main.asm" "level.asm" }

phase intro { needs main  then level }
phase level { needs level  entry run }
entry intro

    main.asm

    .proc entry
        .transition level
.endp

    level.asm

    .section absolute at $4000
map     .byte 1, 2, 3
.ends

.proc run
        lda map
@       jmp @-
.endp

    error[NGA5205]: `map` is loaded from storage, and cannot live where the stream reads through, at $4000
 --> level.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute at $4000
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Only a pin reaches this, since the solver keeps such a Section out of the Window by itself. Drop the pin, or put the Section in a Pane, which has no Payload and is read where it stands. A Section with no Payload pinned in a Window is NGA5235. See Banks and Windows.

    NGA5206

    error · no layout satisfies every constraint at once

    The solver showed that no layout exists. Usually a finding beside it says why: a Phase over capacity (NGA5631, NGA5632), a Pane over its Bank (NGA5225), too little ROM (NGA5234), or a Section with no room at all (NGA5202). Alone, it means that every Section fits on its own and every sum holds, and the constraints together still cannot be met.

    .section absolute align $4000
font    .res $3000
.ends

.section absolute align $4000
screen  .res $3000
.ends

    error[NGA5206]: no layout satisfies every constraint at once

    Both can start only at $4000, since $8000 plus their size runs past the stand-in's memory. Run the build with --explain to have the tool name the pairs no layout keeps apart (NGA5207).

    NGA5207

    error · {section} and {other} cannot be kept apart: no layout holds both without one lying over the other

    Raised only when the build is run with --explain, after NGA5206, and only where no sum already said why. The tool then looks for the layout that lets the fewest pairs of Sections overlap, and names each pair it had to let overlap. Where several choices are equally small, it names one of them. Each Section of a pair gets an NGA5208 note.

    Change one Section of each pair: its size, its align, within or pin, or the Phases its Module is needed in.

    NGA5208

    note · {section} is declared here

    Follows NGA5207, once for each Section of the pair, and points at its declaration.

    NGA5209

    warning · the search stopped before it could show that fewer pairs would do; the ones named suffice

    Follows the NGA5207 findings under --explain when the search for the fewest overlapping pairs ran out of its budget. A layout exists if the pairs named may overlap, but fewer pairs might be enough. Start from them all the same.

    NGA5210

    error · this assertion does not hold

    .assert states a condition checked after Place, when every address and size is known. Raised where the condition is zero.

    .section
colors  .byte $00, $0E, $34, $86, $C8
.ends

.proc entry
        lda colors
        rts
.endp

.assert colors.runtimeSectionSize == 4

    error[NGA5210]: this assertion does not hold
  --> main.asm:10:1
   |
10 | .assert colors.runtimeSectionSize == 4
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    An assertion guards something the code relies on and the solver does not know. Either the program changed under it, or the assertion is out of date.

    NGA5211

    error · this assertion cannot be decided

    Raised where an .assert has no value even after Place. The usual cause is a Section that Prune dropped, which has no address: an .assert is not a Reference, so it does not keep the Section it names. A division whose divisor comes out zero is the other cause.

    .section
table   .byte 1, 2, 3
.ends

.proc entry
        rts
.endp

.assert table >= $2000

    error[NGA5211]: this assertion cannot be decided
 --> main.asm:9:1
  |
9 | .assert table >= $2000
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Nothing reaches table. Name it from code that is kept, mark it root, or remove the assertion.

    NGA5212

    error · an alignment is a declared power of two from 1 to 65,536, and {text} is {what}

    align N takes a declared value that is a power of two from 1 to 65,536: the start of the Section is a multiple of it. Raised for zero, for a larger value, for one that is not a power of two, such as align 3, and for one that is not declared.

    .section absolute align 0
font    .res 1024
.ends

    error[NGA5212]: an alignment is a declared power of two from 1 to 65,536, and `0` is out of that range
 --> main.asm:1:25
  |
1 | .section absolute align 0
  |                         ^

    NGA5213

    error · a boundary is a declared count of bytes from 1 to 65,536, and {text} is {what}

    within N takes a declared value from 1 to 65,536, as align does (NGA5212), but need not be a power of two: the Section does not cross a multiple of it. within 256 keeps a Section in one page.

    .section absolute within 0
list    .res 32
.ends

    error[NGA5213]: a boundary is a declared count of bytes from 1 to 65,536, and `0` is out of that range
 --> main.asm:1:26
  |
1 | .section absolute within 0
  |                          ^

    NGA5214

    error · {section} is {size:n} bytes, and cannot lie within a boundary of {boundary:n}

    within N keeps a Section from crossing a multiple of N, so the Section can be at most N bytes. Raised before the solver is asked, since no start would do.

    .section absolute within 256
sines   .res 320
.ends

    error[NGA5214]: `sines` is 320 bytes, and cannot lie within a boundary of 256
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute within 256
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Split the Section into parts that each fit, each with its own within, or widen the boundary.

    NGA5215

    error · {section} is pinned at {address:hex}, which is not aligned to {alignment:n}

    A pin has to satisfy the rest of the Section's placement. Here the address after at is not a multiple of the align.

    .section absolute at $3200 align 1024
font    .res 1024
.ends

    error[NGA5215]: `font` is pinned at $3200, which is not aligned to 1,024
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute at $3200 align 1024
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Move the pin to a multiple, or drop the at and let the solver choose an aligned address.

    NGA5216

    error · {section} is pinned at {address:hex}, and reaches {last:hex} across a boundary of {boundary:n}

    A pinned Section with within N must not cross a multiple of N. This pin starts close enough to one that the Section's last byte lies past it.

    .section absolute at $33F0 within 1024
dlist   .res 32
.ends

    error[NGA5216]: `dlist` is pinned at $33F0, and reaches $340F across a boundary of 1,024
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute at $33F0 within 1024
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Move the pin, or drop the at and let the solver find a start that keeps the Section inside the boundary.

    NGA5217

    error · {section} is pinned at {address:hex}, in the register region {region}, where nothing can be placed

    A register Region is hardware, and nothing the program places can stand there. A pin into one is an error, where a pin into a reserved Region is a warning (NGA5218).

    main.ngp

    target {
  region $0080 .. $00FF ram
  region $2000 .. $BFFF ram
  region gtia $D000 .. $D01F register
}

modules { "main.asm" }

    main.asm

    .section absolute at $D000
hposp0  .res 1
hposp1  .res 1
.ends

    error[NGA5217]: `hposp0` is pinned at $D000, in the register region `gtia`, where nothing can be placed
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute at $D000
  | ^^^^^^^^
note: the region `gtia` is declared here
 --> main.ngp:4:3
  |
4 |   region gtia $D000 .. $D01F register
  |   ^^^^^^

    Name a register in the target block instead, as register HPOSP0 $D000, and every Module sees the name; see the Project file. Memory that another chip reads, such as a Lynx display buffer over Mikey's registers, is declared foreign and root, and may lie there.

    NGA5218

    warning · {section} is pinned at {address:hex}, in the reserved region {region}

    A reserved Region belongs to something else, usually the machine or its DOS. A pin puts a Section there anyway, which the tool allows and reports. Read it as a question: is this Region really reserved, or is this pin really wanted.

    main.ngp

    target {
  region $0080 .. $00FF ram
  region dos $0700 .. $1FFF reserved
  region $2000 .. $BFFF ram
}

modules { "main.asm" }

    main.asm

    .section absolute at $0700
buffer  .res 16
.ends

.proc entry
        lda buffer
        rts
.endp

    warning[NGA5218]: `buffer` is pinned at $0700, in the reserved region `dos`
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section absolute at $0700
  | ^^^^^^^^
note: the region `dos` is declared here
 --> main.ngp:3:3
  |
3 |   region dos $0700 .. $1FFF reserved
  |   ^^^^^^

    Not raised for a foreign Section, nor for a Module the Container's load needs, whose memory the variant reserves for it. A pin into a register Region is an error instead, NGA5217, and so is a pin into a rom Region of a Section that is not read-only, NGA5233.

    NGA5219

    error · the search found no layout within its budget, and no sum shows that none exists

    The solver's search has a budget. Raised where it ran out before finding a layout or showing that none exists, and no sum over a Phase refused the program first. It does not mean that no layout exists. The NGA5220 note names the pool with the least room left, which is where to look first.

    Many pins that cut memory into small holes, with many Sections about the size of those holes, make the search hard. Free some room in the pool the note names, or drop pins and alignments the program does not need. --explain does not run here, since nothing was shown to explain.

    NGA5220

    note · phase {phase} has the least room left in {pool}: {free:n} of {available:n} bytes

    Follows NGA5219. It names the Phase and the pool, view fixed or the zero page, whose sum came closest to refusing the program, and how many of its bytes are free.

    NGA5222

    error · there is no storage for {section}, which needs {size:n} bytes

    A Section with a Payload waits in storage until a Transition loads it, and so does every Frame. Raised where storage has no free run long enough for this one after what was placed before it. The size is that of the stored form, so a transform changes it. A Frame is named by its edge, as frame intro -> level.

    main.ngp

    target {
  region $0080 .. $00FF ram
  region $2000 .. $BFFF ram
  register PORTB $D301
  units extension 1
  window ext $4000 .. $5FFF views extension
}
storage { units extension }

modules { "atari/portb.asm" "main.asm" "level.asm" }
resident { portb }

phase intro { needs main  then level }
phase level { needs level  entry run }
entry intro

    main.asm

    .proc entry
        .transition level
.endp

    level.asm

    .section
map     .byte 1
        .res $2000
        .byte 1
.ends

.proc run
        lda map
@       jmp @-
.endp

    error[NGA5222]: there is no storage for `map`, which needs 8,196 bytes
 --> level.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section
  | ^^^^^^^^

    Storage here is one Bank of 8 KB. Reserved space between two emitted bytes travels with them, so the .res costs storage; at the end of the Section it would cost nothing. Otherwise compress the Section with a transform in the Project, or use a Target with more storage. See the Project file.

    NGA5224

    warning · {section} is root and holds no bytes to restore, and is evicted in phase {gap} {between}

    A root Section is read by the hardware with no Reference in the code. One that only reserves space has no bytes to carry, so where a Phase that does not need its Module comes between two that do, nothing puts its contents back. The later Phase finds what the Phase in between left there.

    main.ngp

    modules { "main.asm" "game.asm" }

phase intro { needs main  then game }
phase game  { needs game  then outro  entry play }
phase outro { needs main  then game  entry finish }
entry intro

    main.asm

    .section root
screen  .res 960
.ends

.proc entry
        .transition game
.endp

.proc finish
@       jmp @-
.endp

    game.asm

    .proc play
        .transition outro
.endp

    warning[NGA5224]: `screen` is `root` and holds no bytes to restore, and is evicted in phase `game` between `intro` and `outro`, which both need it
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section root
  | ^^^^^^^^

    List the Module in game too, or in resident, so that it stays. Where the program sets the memory up again on every entry, .off NGA5224 above the Section says so. A root Section that holds bytes is not reported: its bytes are brought back, or kept in place where there is no storage.

    NGA5225

    error · pane {pane} takes {size:n} bytes in phase {phase}, and a bank of {set} holds {available:n}

    A Pane is one Bank, so its Sections present in one Phase have to fit in it together. The sum is checked before the solver is asked, and the finding points at the Pane. A Project with no phase block has one unnamed Phase, which the message calls (implicit).

    main.ngp

    include "atari/130xe.ngp"

modules { "main.asm" }

panes in ext { level }

    main.asm

    .section in level, root
map     .res $3000
.ends

.section in level, root
tiles   .res $1800
.ends

    error[NGA5225]: pane `level` takes 18,432 bytes in phase `(implicit)`, and a bank of `extension` holds 16,384
 --> main.ngp:5:1
  |
5 | panes in ext { level }
  | ^^^^^

error[NGA5206]: no layout satisfies every constraint at once

    Declare a second Pane, panes in ext { level, tiles }, and move one Section to it, or put the two in Modules no Phase needs together. NGA5206 follows, as it follows every sum that refuses.

    NGA5226

    error · {section} is pinned at {address:hex}, outside the window of pane {pane}

    A Pane's Section is reached through its Pane's Window, which is the only place its Bank appears. A pin must put the whole Section inside the Window's ranges.

    main.ngp

    include "atari/130xe.ngp"

modules { "main.asm" }

panes in ext { level }

    main.asm

    .section in level, absolute at $8000, root
map     .res 1024
.ends

    error[NGA5226]: `map` is pinned at $8000, outside the window of pane `level`
 --> main.asm:1:1
  |
1 | .section in level, absolute at $8000, root
  | ^^^^^^^^

    ext is $4000-$7FFF on the 130XE. Pin inside it, or drop the pin and let the solver choose where in the Window the Section stands.

    NGA5227

    error · {section} has bytes and is in pane {pane}, which is pinned to a named state: only a .xex fills one, and only in the window its driver's stream reads through

    A named state is not a Bank: storage holds nothing for it, and outside the case the message names, no Container writes bytes into it. A Pane pinned to one holds reservations, which the program fills itself.

    main.ngp

    include "atari/mariacel.ngp"

modules { "main.asm" }

panes in cel4000 = derived { shapes }

container xex

A finding of it means the tool placed something wrong. The program is not at fault, and there is nothing in it to change. Report the finding with the Project that raised it. The option changes nothing in the build, so a build without it writes the same Layout with the same fault.

    This one finds two Sections on a common address in a Phase that holds both. Two Temporaries that are never live at once may share an address, and so may two Sections in different states of one Window. This pair is neither.

The same rule for a pin is NGA5205.

What an index register adds at run time is not checked, nor is an access through a pointer, and taking the address with #< is not an access.

    target {
  region     $0080 .. $00FF  ram
  region     $0200 .. $FBFF  ram

    A driver that declares .driver span none has such a form cut into pieces that each fit in a track. The shipped pet/disk.asm declares it. A driver of your own for a diskette that does not declare it gets the form whole, and no track holds it. Add .driver span none to the driver.

Those bytes past the end must be memory the loader may write while the file loads: in a ram Region, and not held by a root reservation of the entry Phase, such as the OS ROM, or by a Module of the load block. Raised when they are not. The .xex then carries the Section's bytes as they are.

    include "atari/800xl.ngp"

Raised when no free stretch is large enough to hold any of them. Free means clear of every root reservation of the entry Phase, of what the load block says the machine holds, and of the driver and the tool's own load code. Reserve less in the entry Phase, so that some memory is free while the program loads.

Raised when the form is larger than the largest free stretch. The Section is then moved as it is, in pieces, and the .xex is larger by what the encoding would have saved. Reserve less in the entry Phase, or take the Section out of the transform block.

    Raised when the Container is bs93 and a Section has a Payload, which waits in storage for a Transition to load it. An emulator copies a bs93 block into memory and enters it, and nothing ever reads storage.

    main.ngp

    include "lynx/lynx.ngp"
include "lynx/cart64k.ngp"

modules { "intro.asm" "level.asm" }

phase intro { needs intro  then level  entry introStart }
phase level { needs level              entry levelStart }
entry intro

container bs93

    intro.asm

    .proc introStart
        .transition level
.endp

    level.asm

    .section
map     .byte 1, 2, 3
.ends

.proc levelStart
        lda map
@stop   bra @stop
.endp

  |
1 | .section
  | ^^^^^^^^

error[NGA6235]: `levelStart` waits in storage, and a `bs93` image is one block an emulator copies into memory: it has no loader, and nothing would ever put those bytes where they belong
 --> level.asm:5:1
  |
5 | .proc levelStart
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Leave out the storage document, here lynx/cart64k.ngp. Without storage every Section with bytes is in the block, and a Transition loads nothing. Or build a cartridge, container lnx "64k", which has a loader.

    NGA6236

    error · a Lynx cartridge is booted by fifty bytes its ROM decrypts and the loader they read in, and those were not made

    A Lynx cartridge boots in two parts. The boot ROM decrypts fifty bytes from the start of the cartridge and runs them, and they read the rest of the loader, which reads the program. The tool writes both parts itself, as a Module of its own, and fills in two operands of the second part. Raised when that Module or those operands are missing. It is a check of the tool's own work, and nothing a Project declares is meant to reach it.

    NGA6237

    error · the boot ROM decrypts {available:n} bytes and the loader's first part came to {required:n}

    The first part of a Lynx cartridge's loader is the one block the boot ROM decrypts, fifty bytes run at $0200. Raised when the tool's own first part comes to more. It is a check of the tool's work rather than of the program's.

    NGA6238

    error · the rest of page zero holds {available:n} bytes and the loader came to {required:n}: the first part reads the second where the ROM left the counter, and the counter does not leave the page it is on

    The second part of a Lynx cartridge's loader stands in the rest of page zero, after the first part. The first part reads it from where the boot ROM's counter stopped, and the counter does not run on into the next page, so the loader has to fit in that page: 204 bytes on a 64k board. Raised when it does not. The loader is the tool's own and is written to fit the smallest board, so this is a check of the tool's work.

    NGA6239

    error · a {name} cartridge holds {available:n} bytes and this comes to {required:n}

    Raised when a Lynx cartridge would need more bytes than the board holds. Page zero holds the loader, storage follows from page one, and the load image, which is everything the entry Phase needs, begins on the page after the storage the program uses. The message counts all three. Here the entry Phase carries 40000 bytes and the other Phase's 30000 wait in storage.

    main.ngp

    include "lynx/lynx.ngp"
include "lynx/cart64k.ngp"

modules { "intro.asm" "level.asm"
  script( "fill.js", name = "title", size = 40000 ) as titleArt
  script( "fill.js", name = "map", size = 30000 ) as levelArt
}

phase intro { needs intro, titleArt  then level  entry introStart }
phase level { needs level, levelArt              entry levelStart }
entry intro

container lnx "64k"

    fill.js

    export default ( args ) => ( {
  sections: [ { name: args.name, items: [ new Uint8Array( args.size ) ] } ]
} );

    intro.asm

    .proc introStart
        lda title
        .transition level
.endp

    level.asm

    .proc levelStart
        lda map
@stop   bra @stop
.endp

    error[NGA6239]: a `64k` cartridge holds 65,536 bytes and this comes to 70,895

    Name a larger board, "128k", "256k" or "512k", and include its storage document in place of lynx/cart64k.ngp. Or make the Payloads smaller with a transform.

    NGA6240

    error · a prg is loaded at BASIC's own start and the line that enters it stands there, so the program begins at {floor:hex}: this image begins at {begin:hex}, which the load would write over BASIC's pointers

    Raised when the Container is prg and the image begins below $040E. LOAD puts a .prg at BASIC's start, $0401, and the tool puts a line of BASIC there that enters the program with SYS. The program's own bytes begin behind that line. A Section with bytes further down would have to be loaded over BASIC's pointers by the load itself.

    main.ngp

    include "pet/3032.ngp"

modules { "main.asm" }

container prg

    main.asm

    .section zeropage
speed   .byte 4
.ends

.proc entry
        lda speed
        rts
.endp

    error[NGA6240]: a `prg` is loaded at BASIC's own start and the line that enters it stands there, so the program begins at $040E: this image begins at $00, which the load would write over BASIC's pointers

    pet/3032.ngp leaves $0200-$040D out of every Region, so the solver keeps out of it. The cause is a pin or, as here, a zeropage Section with bytes. Reserve the byte with .res 1 and set it from code.

    NGA6241

    error · {section} waits in storage, and a prg is one block a PET is handed by hand: it has no loader, and nothing would ever put those bytes where they belong

    main.ngp

    include "pet/3032.ngp"
include "pet/d64.ngp"

modules { "intro.asm" "level.asm" }

phase intro { needs intro  then level  entry introStart }
phase level { needs level              entry levelStart }
entry intro

container prg

    intro.asm

    .proc introStart
        .transition level
.endp

    level.asm

    .section
map     .byte 1, 2, 3
.ends

.proc levelStart
        lda map
@stop   jmp @stop
.endp

  |
5 | .proc levelStart
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Build the same program as container d64, the diskette whose other sectors a Transition reads. Or leave out the storage document, here pet/d64.ngp: every Section then stays in memory, and a Transition loads nothing.

    NGA6242

    error · the program comes to {required:n} sectors and the Phases left {available:n}: a diskette holds both, and the Phases are placed first

    Raised when a Commodore diskette, d64, d80 or d82, has too few free sectors left for the program's own file. The Phases' storage is written first. The program, the file LOAD reads, then goes into what is left as a chain of sectors, 254 bytes of it in each. The message counts the sectors the program needs and those left.

    Make the Payloads smaller with a transform, or use a larger surface, d80 or d82, with the storage document of that surface.

    NGA6243

    error · the program has no bytes, and a {container} of none would load nothing

    Raised when the Container is prg, d64 or bs93 and the entry Phase has no Section that writes a byte. Each of them is one block that a machine loads and then enters, and a block of nothing has nothing to enter.

    main.ngp

    modules { "main.asm" }

container prg

    main.asm

    .proc entry
.endp

    error[NGA6243]: the program has no bytes, and a `prg` of none would load nothing

    Give the entry Phase the code it runs. A raw image of the same program is an empty file, which is all such a program is, so a raw image is not refused.

    NGA6244

    error · the tool wrote no {container} and found nothing wrong with the program: the fault is the tool's

    Raised when a Container came out with no bytes and nothing the tool checked said why. Every other refusal of a Container names its reason. This one stands for the places where writing stops on something an earlier Step should have ruled out, such as a Label the tool declared itself and then cannot find. It is a check of the tool's own work, and nothing a Project declares is meant to reach it. Report it with the Project that raised it. Without this check the tool would write an empty file and report success.

    include "atari/800xl.ngp"

load { needs detect  init detect }

phase main { needs main }
entry main

container xex

    low.ngp

    constants { LEVEL = 1 }

    high.ngp

    constants { LEVEL = 2 }

    detect.asm

    .proc detect
        lda #1
        sta ngaChoice
        rts
.endp

    main.asm

    .proc entry
.if LEVEL == 1
        lda #1
.else
        lda #1
        ora #2
.endif

        rts
.endp

.section
level   .res 1
.ends

    NGA7001

    error · unexpected character {character}

    The lexer found a character, outside a comment or a literal, that no token of C begins with: $, @, a backtick, a \, or a letter beyond ASCII in a name. A name is ASCII letters, digits and _.

    static u8 total;

static void entry()
{
  total = $10;
}

 --> main.ngc:5:11
  |
5 |   total = $10;
  |           ^

    $ is the assembler's prefix for hexadecimal. C writes 0x10. A character beyond ASCII belongs in a literal that names a Charset, see NGA7016. A byte that is not valid UTF-8 is reported here too when it stands outside a comment or a literal; inside one it is NGA7003.

    NGA7002

    error · control character {code:hex} in source

    The lexer found a byte below $20 other than tab, line feed and carriage return, or the byte $7F, between tokens or inside a string literal or a character constant. A form feed or a vertical tab is not whitespace here. Refusing these bytes means that a file that is not text, such as a binary named as a .ngc or a source saved as UTF-16, stops here and is not read as tokens. Inside a literal, a raw tab is allowed, as it is in an assembler string.

    Delete the character, or save the file as UTF-8. A byte that should be in a string is written as an escape, such as \n, or as a number in a u8 array. A comment may hold a control character. The line quoted under the message shows the byte as its symbol from Unicode's Control Pictures, ␀ for a NUL.

    NGA7003

    error · invalid UTF-8 encoding

    A comment or a literal holds bytes that are not UTF-8. Source is UTF-8. A file saved in an 8-bit code page, such as Windows-1250, or text exported from an Atari editor, has bytes above $7F that are not valid UTF-8. A comment reports this once, a literal at each bad byte.

    Convert the file to UTF-8. Outside a comment or a literal, such a byte is NGA7001.

    NGA7004

    error · /* is not closed before the end of the file

    A block comment runs to the first */, and there is none before the end of the file. Usually the */ was deleted, or a comment opened to disable some code was never closed.

    static u8 total;

/* Clears the total.
static void clear()
{
  total = 0;
}

 --> main.ngc:3:1

3 | /* Clears the total.
  | ^^

    // Converted from C:\ART\

 --> main.ngc:1:25

1 | // Converted from C:\ART\

    error · a literal of {second} is not joined to one of {first}

    Adjacent string literals join into one, as in C, only where they carry the same prefix. No prefix counts as a prefix of its own: ASCII, untranslated. C would give the joined literal the one prefix written; the subset refuses the join.

    main.ngp

    include "atari/800xl.ngp"

modules { "main.ngc" }

    main.ngc

    static u8 const title[] = "SCORE " screen"000";

    error[NGA7103]: a literal of `screen` is not joined to one of no prefix
 --> main.ngc:1:36
  |
1 | static u8 const title[] = "SCORE " screen"000";
  |                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^

    Give every piece the same prefix: screen"SCORE " screen"000".

    NGA7200

    error · the compiler does not compile {construct} yet

    The grammar reads more of C than the compiler compiles. A construct that parses and has no code behind it is refused where it stands, and the message names it. Among them are a call of anything but a name, an assignment to anything but a name, an expression statement that neither assigns nor calls, a constant shifted by a value, and any operator on a pointer but +, -, == and !=.

    static u8 x;
static u8 y;

static void entry()
{
  x = 1 << y;
}

 --> main.ngc:6:7
  |
6 |   x = 1 << y;
  |       ^^^^^^

    Rewrite it with what compiles, here as x = 1; followed by x <<= y;. See Statements and expressions.

    NGA7201

    A name needs no declaration before its use, and most names are visible to the whole program. A static name is seen only in its own file, a name of an assembler Module only where that Module .exports it, and a local only in its block or in the statement that declares it. The Charset before a literal is a name too.

    main.ngc

    static u8 shown;

static void entry()
{
  reset();
  shown = lives;
}

    other.ngc

    static u8 lives;

void reset()
{
  lives = 3;
}

 --> main.ngc:6:11
  |
6 |   shown = lives;
  |           ^^^^^

    Only a C function or an assembler .proc can be called. Raised for a call of an object, a type, or a name the assembler exports that is not a Proc, such as a Label over code in a .section. A Proc says what it takes and returns through its .declare lines. A Label says nothing about either.

    main.ngc

    static void entry()
{
  clear();
}

    clear.asm

    .export clear

.section
clear   lda #0
        sta $0600
        rts
.ends

 --> main.ngc:3:3
  |
3 |   clear();
  |   ^^^^^

    Write the routine as .proc clear and .endp, and keep the .export. See Reading the assembler.

    error · {name} is a function, and a function cannot be assigned

    A function's name stands for its code, and code is not assigned. Raised for an assignment to a C function or to an assembler .proc. The usual intent is a handler that changes while the program runs, which is a pointer of a function type.

    static void idle()
{
}

static void update()
{
}

static void entry()
{
  update = idle;
}

  --> main.ngc:11:3
   |
11 |   update = idle;
   |   ^^^^^^

    Declare the handler as a pointer, typedef void step(); and static step* update;, and assign the function to it. See Function types.

    A file defines each name once. Raised for a second object, function, type or enumerator of a name the file defines already, and for a local or a parameter declared twice in one scope. C takes two u8 x; at file scope as one object, and the subset refuses them as well. An enumerator of a plain enum is a name of the file, so it meets the file's other names.

    static u8 score;
static u16 score;

 --> main.ngc:2:12
  |
2 | static u16 score;
  |            ^^^^^
note: the previous definition of `score` is here
 --> main.ngc:1:11
  |
1 | static u8 score;
  |           ^^^^^

    Rename one, or delete the second. While a file has a name defined twice at file scope its bodies are not checked, so more findings may follow the fix. The same name exported by two files is NGA2205.

    NGA7205

    note · the previous definition of {name} is here

    Follows NGA7204, and NGA7271 for a second extern, and points at the first definition of the name.

    NGA7206

    error · {value} is outside the range of {type}

    An integer constant takes its type from where it is used: the object it is assigned to, the parameter it is given to, or the operand beside it. Raised where that type cannot hold it. An expression of constants is folded exactly, and only the answer is held to the type, so 256 - 1 stands where a u8 is wanted and 200 + 100 does not. A - directly before a constant is its sign, so -128 is an i8.

    static u8 timer;

static void entry()
{
  timer = 300;
}

    error[NGA7206]: 300 is outside the range of `u8`
 --> main.ngc:5:11
  |
5 |   timer = 300;
  |           ^^^

    Use a wider type, or a cast where the wrap is meant: (u8)300 is 44. A constant beside a u8 operand is held to u8 even where the result goes into a u16, so widen the operand: (u16)x + 300. In a comparison the same constant is a warning, NGA7210.

    The operands of one operator have one signedness, and so do an object and the value assigned to it. C converts one to the other by its promotion rules, which are easy to misread, so the subset asks for a cast that says which is meant.

    static u8 x;
static i8 dx;

static void entry()
{
  x += dx;
}

 --> main.ngc:6:5
  |
6 |   x += dx;
  |     ^^

    Cast one side. x += (u8)dx; adds the same byte, so a negative dx still moves x down. A wider value assigned to a narrower object is NGA7208.

    NGA7208

    error · a {from} does not fit in the {to} it is assigned to without a cast

    A wider value is not assigned to a narrower object without a cast. C drops the high byte silently; here the cast says that it is meant. Raised for an assignment, an argument and a return. A narrower value is widened where it is assigned, a u8 with zeros and an i8 with its sign, so that direction needs nothing.

    static u16 score;
static u8 low;

static void entry()
{
  low = score;
}

 --> main.ngc:6:9
  |
6 |   low = score;
  |         ^^^^^

    Cast to keep the low byte, low = (u8)score;, or write (u8)(score >> 8) for the high one.

    error · a bool holds true, false or a comparison, and is neither an operand nor an integer

C converts any integer to 0 or 1 on the way into a bool, and the subset has no such conversion. !, && and || take a bool.

    static bool paused;

static void entry()
{
  paused = 0;
}

5 |   paused = 0;

    static u8 table[256];

static void entry()
{

}

 --> main.ngc:5:22

5 |   for (u8 i = 0; i < 256; ++i)

    static u8 high;
static u8 low;

static void entry()
{
  address = high << 8 | low;
}

 --> main.ngc:7:21
  |
7 |   address = high << 8 | low;
  |                     ^

    NGA7212

    error · a condition is a bool, and this is {what}

    The condition of if, while, do, for and ?:, and each operand of !, && and ||, is a bool. C takes any integer or pointer there and tests it against zero. The subset wants the comparison written.

    static u8 frames;

static void entry()
{
  while (1)

}

 --> main.ngc:5:10
  |
5 |   while (1)

    NGA7213

    error · {keyword} stands in no {around}

    continue stands in a loop, and break in a loop or a switch. Raised for one in neither, usually a break meant to leave the function.

{

7 |     break;

 --> main.ngc:1:8

1 | static uint8_t lives;
  |        ^^^^^^^

static void entry()
{
